# Lesson: Relationships

# Relationships

Not every relationship between picos is parent and child. A flower shop may need a link to a delivery driver so it can broadcast a request and the driver can bid on it, and neither created the other. Many systems are built from peers. This lesson teaches picos to link to one another with **relationships**, and to use the link.

> **Terminology:** What the engine now calls a *relationship* was called a *subscription* before engine 1.6.2. The ideas are the same. The ruleset is still `io.picolabs.subscription`, and the older event names (`wrangler:subscription`, `wrangler:pending_subscription_approval`, …) still work next to the new ones. This lesson uses the new names. See [Relationships](/wrangler/relationships) for the full list.

## Objectives

When you finish you will be able to:

- explain what a relationship is: a named, two-way link with a channel and a role at each end
- say what `Tx`, `Rx`, `Tx_role`, `Rx_role`, and the well-known channel are
- create, approve, and inspect relationships in the developer UI
- create, approve, reject, and cancel relationships from rules
- send an event over a relationship and use it to tell friend from stranger
- say what changes when a relationship uses DIDs instead of a well-known channel

**Before you begin**, finish:

- [Quickstart](/lessons/quickstart): install rulesets
- [Events and Queries](/lessons/events-and-queries): channels, and events raised on them
- [Pico State](/lessons/pico-state): entity variables, simple and complex
- [Pico-Based Systems](/lessons/pico-based-systems): create and delete children, and install rulesets in them (you'll rebuild the registration system from it here)

and read [Relationships](/wrangler/relationships) in the Wrangler documentation.

## Relationships

A relationship has a name and **two channels**, one owned by each pico. Each pico sees it from its own side. In a relationship between picos A and B:

- A's **`Rx`** is the channel on which A *receives* events and queries. It's a channel in A, and its policy decides what B may do. It's B's `Tx`.
- A's **`Tx`** is the channel A *transmits* on, to reach B. It's B's `Rx`.

The two picos see the channels swapped, which is the point: each side keeps its own rules about who can do what to it.

Each end may also have a role. From A's perspective, **`Rx_role`** is A's role, "mine", and **`Tx_role`** is B's, "theirs". From B's perspective they are the other way round. Roles label a relationship (`student`, `section`, `owner`). They prove nothing. What a pico may do is decided by the policy of its `Rx` channel.

The relationship also has an **`Id`**, the same on both ends. It is the one field that is: there's one relationship with two ends, and the rest of its fields swap.

## The experiment

We continue the registration example. The root pico has two children, the **Registration** pico and the **Section Collection** pico. The Section Collection pico has a child pico for each section. Students are children of the Registration pico, and each student will have a relationship with each section they take:

```
 root pico
   ├── Registration pico
   │      └── Student pico (Jane)
   └── Section Collection pico
          ├── Section A HTG 100-1 pico
          └── Section CS462-1 pico
```

Parent-child links are the tree. Relationships are separate lines drawn across it: Jane to a section, and Jane to the Section Collection.

To prepare, (re)build the registration system from [Pico-Based Systems](/lessons/pico-based-systems): install `app_section_collection` in the Section Collection pico and create two sections with `section:needed`. Then create a pico for a student, a child of the root named "Jane", with the About tab. Every pico has `io.picolabs.subscription` installed already, so you needn't install it.

## Create a relationship by hand

To form a relationship, Wrangler makes a new channel in each pico. To get started, it needs a channel that already exists in each one. That's the **well-known channel**.

### Find the well-known channel

Every pico has a **well-known channel**, created by `io.picolabs.subscription` when it's installed. Its policy is deliberately narrow: it accepts only the events that start a relationship (and one that removes an unaccepted request), and it answers a single query, for its own ID. That makes its ECI safe to pass around widely.

Visit a section pico and open its **Relationships** tab. The **Identity** panel shows the well-known channel, `wellKnown_Rx`. Copy it.

### Ask for a relationship

Open Jane's **Relationships** tab and find **New relationship**. Choose the classic (ECI) form and fill it in:

1. `wellKnown_Tx`: paste the section pico's well-known ECI
2. `Rx_role`: this pico's role: `student`
3. `Tx_role`: the other pico's role: `class`
4. `name`: a name for the relationship, such as `Jane-A HTG 100-1`
5. Leave the `channel_type` as it is (the default is `Tx_Rx`), and leave the password and host blank. A password is for auto-accept configuration, and the host is for a pico on another engine

Submit the form. It raises `wrangler:relationship` in Jane's pico.

### Look at what happened

On Jane's **Channels** tab there's a new channel for this relationship. It is Jane's `Rx`, and the section's `Tx`. On Jane's **Relationships** tab, the relationship is under **Outbound pending**: proposed to the other pico, not yet accepted.

Visit the section pico. Its **Inbound pending** list has the same relationship. Expand both and compare. `Id` is the same. The roles are swapped and so are `Tx` and `Rx`. Jane doesn't yet have the section's ECI, because the section hasn't accepted.

### Accept it

On the section pico, expand the inbound relationship and click **Approve**. That raises `wrangler:pending_relationship_approval` with the relationship's `Id`. Both sides now show it as **Established**. Jane has the section's channel, and the section has Jane's.

Do it again with Jane and the other section. Jane's established list now has two relationships. Their `Id`s differ.

## Create a relationship from a rule

Everything the UI did, a rule can do, so the system can build itself. The challenge is the starting point: a rule can only use a well-known ECI that it has *found*. Someone must publish it. A natural place is the parent: a new pico tells its parent, and others ask the parent.

### Sections report their well-known channels

Replace `app_section` from the last lesson with this version. Its rule runs when the ruleset is installed, finds the pico's well-known channel, and tells the Section Collection pico:

```krl
ruleset app_section {
  meta {
    name "Section"
    use module io.picolabs.wrangler alias wrangler
    use module io.picolabs.subscription alias relationship
    shares sectionId
  }
  global {
    sectionId = function() {
      ent:section_id
    }
  }

  rule pico_ruleset_added {
    select when wrangler ruleset_installed where event:attr("rids") >< meta:rid
    pre {
      section_id = event:attr("section_id")
      well_known = relationship:wellKnown_Rx(){"id"}
    }
    event:send({
      "eci": wrangler:parent_eci(),
      "domain": "section",
      "type": "identify",
      "attrs": {"section_id": section_id, "wellKnown_eci": well_known}
    })
    always {
      ent:section_id := section_id
    }
  }
}
```

Look at the new parts: the `use module io.picolabs.subscription alias relationship` line gives access to the relationship functions. `relationship:wellKnown_Rx()` returns the well-known channel, a map with an `id`. `event:send` in the action block sends `section:identify` to the parent over the family channel.

Add these rules to `app_section_collection`. The first one stores what sections report:

```krl
rule accept_wellKnown {
  select when section identify
    section_id re#(.+)#
    wellKnown_eci re#(.+)#
    setting(section_id, wellKnown_eci)
  always {
    ent:sections{[section_id, "wellKnown_eci"]} := wellKnown_eci
  }
}

// A student asked for a relationship with this pico: this pico's role is registration.
rule accept_student {
  select when wrangler inbound_pending_relationship_added
    where event:attr("Rx_role") == "registration"
  always {
    raise wrangler event "pending_relationship_approval" attributes event:attrs
  }
}

rule introduce_section_to_student {
  select when section add_request
  pre {
    section_id = event:attr("section_id")
    name = event:attr("name")
  }
  event:send({
    "eci": ent:sections{[section_id, "wellKnown_eci"]},
    "domain": "wrangler",
    "type": "relationship",
    "attrs": {
      "wellKnown_Tx": event:attr("wellKnown_Tx"),
      "Rx_role": "section",
      "Tx_role": "student",
      "name": name + "-" + section_id,
      "section_id": section_id
    }
  })
}
```

After a few sections have reported, `sections()` returns more than it did, because each entry now has the section's well-known ECI beside its family `eci`:

```json
{
  "CS462-1": { "eci": "cm0a8w4ks0004m8ys0p1e5k2r", "wellKnown_eci": "cm0a8w4ls0007m8ys6bd2f5h3" },
  "A HTG 100-1": { "eci": "cm0a8w9sd0008m8ysg2l73c1d", "wellKnown_eci": "cm0a8w9tc000bm8ysd4w9j8e1" }
}
```

Any section ID can now be turned into a well-known ECI by asking the Section Collection pico.

The Registration pico has to know the Section Collection pico's well-known channel too. To keep this lesson short, do that by hand: copy it from the Section Collection pico's Relationships tab, and send `registration:collection_known` with the `wellKnown_Rx` attribute to the Registration pico on its Testing tab. (Making the collection report it, like the sections do, is an exercise.)

### The Registration pico makes students

Here is `app_registration`. When a student arrives, it creates a child pico for them. When the child has finished setting up, it installs `app_student` and passes along the student's name and the collection's well-known channel:

```krl
ruleset app_registration {
  meta {
    use module io.picolabs.wrangler alias wrangler
    shares collection
  }
  global {
    collection = function() {
      ent:collectionWellKnown
    }
  }

  rule collection_known {
    select when registration collection_known wellKnown_Rx re#(.+)# setting(well_known)
    always {
      ent:collectionWellKnown := well_known
    }
  }

  rule allow_student_to_register {
    select when student arrives name re#(.+)# setting(name)
    always {
      raise wrangler event "new_child_request" attributes {
        "name": name,
        "backgroundColor": event:attr("backgroundColor") || "#CCCCCC",
        "student_name": name
      }
    }
  }

  rule install_student_ruleset {
    select when wrangler child_initialized where event:attr("student_name")
    event:send({
      "eci": event:attr("eci"),
      "domain": "wrangler",
      "type": "install_ruleset_request",
      "attrs": {
        "absoluteURL": meta:rulesetURI,
        "rid": "app_student",
        "student_name": event:attr("student_name"),
        "collection_wellKnown": ent:collectionWellKnown
      }
    })
  }
}
```

This is the same create-then-install chain as in [Pico-Based Systems](/lessons/pico-based-systems): `new_child_request`, then `child_initialized`, then `install_ruleset_request`. Install `app_registration` in the Registration pico, with `app_student` in the same folder. Send `registration:collection_known` first, so there's a well-known channel to pass on, and then `student:arrives` with `name=Jane` on its Testing tab.

### The student asks the collection for a relationship

Now `app_student`, in full. Each rule is explained below, but read the first two now:

```krl
ruleset app_student {
  meta {
    use module io.picolabs.wrangler alias wrangler
    use module io.picolabs.subscription alias relationship
    shares classes
  }
  global {
    classes = function() {
      ent:classes.defaultsTo({}).values()
    }
  }

  rule capture_initial_state {
    select when wrangler ruleset_installed where event:attr("rids") >< meta:rid
    always {
      ent:name := event:attr("student_name")
      ent:collectionWellKnown := event:attr("collection_wellKnown")
      raise student event "new_relationship_request"
    }
  }

  rule make_a_relationship {
    select when student new_relationship_request
    always {
      raise wrangler event "relationship" attributes {
        "wellKnown_Tx": ent:collectionWellKnown,
        "Rx_role": "student",
        "Tx_role": "registration",
        "name": ent:name + "-registration"
      }
    }
  }

  rule add_a_class {
    select when section add_request section_id re#(.+)# setting(section_id)
    pre {
      already_enrolled = classes() >< section_id
      registration = relationship:established("Tx_role", "registration").head()
    }
    if not already_enrolled && registration then
      event:send({
        "sub": registration,
        "domain": "section",
        "type": "add_request",
        "attrs": {
          "wellKnown_Tx": relationship:wellKnown_Rx(){"id"},
          "section_id": section_id,
          "name": ent:name
        }
      })
  }

  rule auto_accept_section {
    select when wrangler inbound_pending_relationship_added
      Rx_role re#^student$#
      Tx_role re#^section$#
    pre {
      section_id = event:attr("section_id")
    }
    if section_id then noop()
    fired {
      ent:classes{event:attr("Id")} := section_id
      raise wrangler event "pending_relationship_approval" attributes event:attrs
      last
    }
  }

  rule reject_everything_else {
    select when wrangler inbound_pending_relationship_added
    always {
      raise wrangler event "inbound_rejection" attributes event:attrs
    }
  }

  rule drop_a_class {
    select when section drop_request section_id re#(.+)# setting(section_id)
    pre {
      rel_id = ent:classes.defaultsTo({})
        .filter(function(v) { v == section_id })
        .keys()
        .head()
    }
    if rel_id then noop()
    fired {
      clear ent:classes{rel_id}
      raise wrangler event "relationship_cancellation" attributes {"Id": rel_id}
    }
  }
}
```

`capture_initial_state` runs when `app_student` is installed in the new pico. It stores what it was given, and raises `student:new_relationship_request`. It's a separate rule so we can raise that event again whenever we need another relationship. `make_a_relationship` raises `wrangler:relationship` with the collection's `wellKnown_Tx`, and roles: this pico is a `student`, the other a `registration`. It's what you did in the UI with the form.

Note what it sends to whom. The student asks the Section Collection pico, and that pico's `accept_student` rule (above) approves any request in which its own role is `registration`:

```krl
rule accept_student {
  select when wrangler inbound_pending_relationship_added
    where event:attr("Rx_role") == "registration"
  always {
    raise wrangler event "pending_relationship_approval" attributes event:attrs
  }
}
```

When a relationship arrives, Wrangler raises `wrangler:inbound_pending_relationship_added` with the attributes of the request, seen from the receiver's side: `Rx_role` is the receiver's own role. The rule approves by raising `wrangler:pending_relationship_approval` with the same attributes (which include `Id`). That's the programmatic version of clicking **Approve**.

Don't approve everyone. This rule only accepts the request when its `Rx_role` is `registration`; anything else is left pending. For something more general, see [Accepting relationship requests](/developing/accepting-relationship-requests) for the auto-accept configuration.

### Add a class: introduce a section

With the relationship between a student and the collection established, a student pico can ask to join a class. The rule `add_a_class` in `app_student`, which you've seen in the listing, sends `section:add_request` over the relationship:

```krl
rule add_a_class {
  select when section add_request section_id re#(.+)# setting(section_id)
  pre {
    already_enrolled = classes() >< section_id
    registration = relationship:established("Tx_role", "registration").head()
  }
  if not already_enrolled && registration then
    event:send({
      "sub": registration,
      "domain": "section",
      "type": "add_request",
      "attrs": {
        "wellKnown_Tx": relationship:wellKnown_Rx(){"id"},
        "section_id": section_id,
        "name": ent:name
      }
    })
}
```

The prelude checks that we aren't enrolled already (`classes()` is a function defined in the ruleset, and shared), and finds the relationship whose other end is a `registration`. `relationship:established("Tx_role", "registration")` returns the established relationships whose `Tx_role` is that. `event:send` with `"sub"` sends over a relationship, here the one with the collection, so the student needs no ECI of its own for the collection. It passes the student's well-known ECI, the section, and the student's name.

The collection pico gets `section:add_request`. Its `introduce_section_to_student` rule (in the listing above) *introduces* the section to the student. It sends a `wrangler:relationship` event to the **section's** well-known channel, with the **student's** well-known ECI as `wellKnown_Tx`:

```krl
rule introduce_section_to_student {
  select when section add_request
  pre {
    section_id = event:attr("section_id")
    name = event:attr("name")
  }
  event:send({
    "eci": ent:sections{[section_id, "wellKnown_eci"]},
    "domain": "wrangler",
    "type": "relationship",
    "attrs": {
      "wellKnown_Tx": event:attr("wellKnown_Tx"),
      "Rx_role": "section",
      "Tx_role": "student",
      "name": name + "-" + section_id,
      "section_id": section_id
    }
  })
}
```

This is the same as typing in the section pico's New relationship form, but the collection did it on its behalf. The section pico needs no code for it: `io.picolabs.subscription` handles the event, and the section proposes a relationship to the student, who is sent the `section_id` as well. This is **introduction**: a third pico that knows both well-known channels connects two picos that don't know each other.

### The student accepts a section

Back in `app_student`, these rules see the proposal arrive:

```krl
rule auto_accept_section {
  select when wrangler inbound_pending_relationship_added
    Rx_role re#^student$#
    Tx_role re#^section$#
  pre {
    section_id = event:attr("section_id")
  }
  if section_id then noop()
  fired {
    ent:classes{event:attr("Id")} := section_id
    raise wrangler event "pending_relationship_approval" attributes event:attrs
    last
  }
}

rule reject_everything_else {
  select when wrangler inbound_pending_relationship_added
  always {
    raise wrangler event "inbound_rejection" attributes event:attrs
  }
}
```

The first rule is selected only when `Rx_role` is `student` and `Tx_role` is `section`. If the request carries a `section_id`, the rule records the relationship in `ent:classes`, a map from relationship `Id` to section id, and approves. The relationship is now established at both ends.

`last` ends the processing of this event in this ruleset, and it's essential. Both rules select the same event, and rules run in the order they're written, so the accepting rule must come first. If it fired, the rejecting rule must not run, or the student would approve and reject the same request. A request this ruleset doesn't recognize falls to `reject_everything_else`, which raises `wrangler:inbound_rejection` to refuse it.

### A class list

`ent:classes` maps relationship ids to section ids, so the list of classes is its values:

```krl
classes = function() {
  ent:classes.defaultsTo({}).values()
}
```

The function is shared in `meta`. Try the whole flow: send `section:add_request` with `section_id=CS462-1` to Jane's pico, and check `classes`. Jane's Relationships tab now lists the collection and the section.

Notice that `section:add_request` is used twice: a user sends it to a student pico, and the student pico sends it to the collection pico. The registration application is one application, spread across several rulesets, for several kinds of pico. Events with the same name mean the same thing wherever they go.

## Cancel a relationship

Either pico in an established relationship can end it by raising `wrangler:relationship_cancellation` with the relationship's `Id`. Wrangler removes both ends. This rule, in `app_student`, drops a class:

```krl
rule drop_a_class {
  select when section drop_request section_id re#(.+)# setting(section_id)
  pre {
    rel_id = ent:classes.defaultsTo({})
      .filter(function(v) { v == section_id })
      .keys()
      .head()
  }
  if rel_id then noop()
  fired {
    clear ent:classes{rel_id}
    raise wrangler event "relationship_cancellation" attributes {"Id": rel_id}
  }
}
```

The prelude finds the relationship for that section. `filter` keeps the map entries whose value is the section id, `keys()` turns the remaining map into an array of its keys, and `head()` takes the first, or `null` if there's none. If there is one, the postlude removes it from `ent:classes` and asks Wrangler to cancel. The rule in `io.picolabs.subscription` removes both ends. You can see the same with the **Delete relationship** button in the Relationships tab.

To remove every relationship at once, for example before deleting a pico, raise `wrangler:cancel_subscriptions`.

## Use DIDs instead of a well-known ECI

Everything above is **classic** (ECI-based) relationships, and it's fully supported. Engine 1.6 added **DID-based** relationships, which are what new work should use. A pico has a portable identity, its `did:webvh`, and a relationship between two DID-based picos has its own private pairwise identity, a `did:peer`. DIDs work across meshes and engines without sharing an ECI.

What changes in the code:

| | Classic | DID-based |
|--|---------|-----------|
| What the asker needs to know | The other pico's well-known ECI, `relationship:wellKnown_Rx(){"id"}` | The other pico's DID, `wrangler:myDid()` |
| `wrangler:relationship` attributes | `wellKnown_Tx` | `layer2: true` and `target_did` |
| The established relationship has | `Tx` and `Rx` ECIs | `Tx_did` and `Rx_did` |
| Sending an event | `event:send({"sub": rel, …})` | the same, or `event:send({"did": …, …})` |
| Querying | `relationship:queryOnSub(Id, rid, name, args)` | the same, or `wrangler:picoQuery(did, rid, name, args)` |

In this lesson's application, a section would report `wrangler:myDid()` instead of its well-known channel, and a student asks with `"layer2": true, "target_did": the_did`. Approval, roles, `inbound_pending_relationship_added`, `last`, and cancellation are the same. One thing to know: a pico accepts an introduction by DID from a stranger only if its **public intro** is on. Root picos default to on. Child picos default to off, so a student pico that others will reach by DID has to turn it on (`wrangler:set_public_intro` with `enabled`). See [Relationships](/wrangler/relationships) for the details, and for how a relationship works across engines.

## Where to go next

- [Relationships](/wrangler/relationships): DIDs, public intro, routing, across engines, and the whole API
- [Two picos talking](/cookbook/two_picos/): two picos, a relationship, and queries over it, that you can run in two minutes
- [Accepting relationship requests](/developing/accepting-relationship-requests): auto-accept by configuration
- [Scatter-Gather](/lessons/scatter-gather): what to do once a pico has relationships with many others

# Lesson: Scatter-Gather

# Scatter-Gather

Sometimes one pico needs many others to do something, and then needs all the answers together. A fleet pico wants a report from every vehicle pico. A course pico wants a grade from every section. A coordinator wants a vote from every member.

The **scatter-gather** pattern does this with events alone, so nobody waits on anybody. This lesson explains the pattern with the problem that taught it to us, and builds a runnable version.

## Objectives

When you finish you will be able to:

- explain why a synchronous request-response solution breaks as the number of picos grows
- scatter an event to a computed list of picos, and gather the answers with an aggregator
- use a **correlation number** to keep concurrent conversations apart
- add a timeout, and say why it is a safety net and not the way the work finishes
- compare event recipient lists, content-based routing, and registration as ways to decide who gets an event

**Before you begin**, finish [Pico-Based Systems](/lessons/pico-based-systems) and [Relationships](/lessons/relationships). The example sends events to children, and the routing examples use relationships.

## The problem

Fuse was an open-source connected-car platform built with picos. Every week it sent the fleet owner a report: the trips and fuel fill-ups of each vehicle in the period, summed for each vehicle and then for the fleet. The owner was a pico, so was the fleet, and so was each vehicle. Each was independent and addressable, kept its own data, and answered queries (functions) and events (rules). They talked to one another directly, with nothing in between.

## The synchronous solution

The straightforward way is for the fleet to *ask* each vehicle for its details, wait for every reply, format the report, and tell the owner that it's ready:

```krl
fleetDetails = function() {
  wrangler:children().map(function(vehicle) {
    wrangler:picoQuery(vehicle{"eci"}, "com.example.vehicle", "summary", {})
  })
}
```

Programmers who've used an API will find that familiar. It works so long as every vehicle answers promptly. A query waits for its answer, so the fleet pico is stuck for the sum of all the delays, and it can't handle anything else meanwhile. Vehicles on other engines are queried over the network, where timeouts have to be short, and one slow vehicle gets missed. With a few vehicles that's rare. With ten, the chance that at least one is late gets good, and with a hundred it's routine.

Longer timeouts only hide the problem. Making each vehicle faster helps, but there is always something that can be slow: the network, a busy engine, a database. If a synchronous request-response were your only tool, this would be a serious problem. It isn't your only tool.

## The scatter-gather solution

Use events, and let every pico work at its own pace. Vaughn Vernon describes the pattern in *Reactive Messaging Patterns with the Actor Model*: get a number of actors to do something, then aggregate what they send back. Here:

1. The owner (or anything else) sends the fleet `report:requested`. Having sent it, the sender is free to do other things.
2. A rule in the fleet **scatters** a `report:vehicle_report_requested` event to each vehicle, whether there are 1 or 100. These are asynchronous too, and under no time pressure.
3. Each vehicle builds its report and sends `report:vehicle_report_created` to the fleet.
4. A rule in the fleet **gathers** them, one at a time, as they arrive.
5. Another rule checks whether every vehicle has answered. When all have, the fleet finishes the report.

There are no queries in this flow, only events. Events go to a pico, not to a particular rule: each pico has its own event bus, and any rule that selects the event runs. A rule doesn't need to know who raised the event, or what else is listening.

## The messy details

Two problems have to be solved for this to be reliable.

**Overlap.** A second report might start before the first has finished. Each run therefore carries a unique **correlation number**, `rcn`. Every rule that sees it passes it along and files its data under it, so two reports in flight at once never get mixed up. (Reports run once a week and almost never overlap, but it's a good habit: independent conversations should be kept independent.)

**Loss.** The "is everyone in?" check depends on events from vehicles. Delivery isn't guaranteed: a pico might be down, an engine unreachable, a pico deleted mid-conversation. If one never answers, the report never finishes. There are several tactics:

- Accept it: tell owners that a report sometimes fails, and let someone ask for it again.
- Set a timeout and carry on, producing the report with some vehicles missing.
- Set a timeout and re-send the request to the vehicles that haven't answered, and give up (carry on without them) after some number of retries.

Fuse used the second. Picos have no clock tick of their own. They react to events, so if you need a timer you schedule an event for later. Two minutes was plenty. Scheduling a short, recurring event to make a "tick" is possible, but usually unnecessary and wasteful.

> **The timeout is a safety net.** The normal path is driven entirely by events: the last answer arrives, the check fires, the report finishes. The timer only matters when something went wrong. Don't schedule an event to wait for work to finish. Chain steps with events instead.

## The pieces

Here is the fleet. It's a ruleset for a pico whose children are vehicles. The rules appear in the order they run, one for each step above.

### Correlating events

A **correlation identifier** links the two halves of an asynchronous conversation. It is an event attribute, any string that's unique within the conversation, and the sender of the first event expects it back in the reply. Rules also use it as a key in persistent state, so each conversation's data is separate.

```krl
// 1. Start: correlate the work, remember who we expect, set a safety timer.
rule start_report {
  select when report requested
  pre {
    rcn = event:attr("rcn") || random:uuid()
    expected = vehicles().map(function(v) { v{"name"} })
  }
  always {
    ent:reports{rcn} := {"expected": expected, "received": {}}
    raise report event "scatter" attributes {"rcn": rcn}
    schedule report event "timer_expired"
      at time:add(time:now(), {"minutes": 2})
      attributes {"rcn": rcn}
  }
}
```

- `rcn` is taken from the event if the caller supplied one (so a retry can reuse a number), and otherwise generated with `random:uuid()`.
- The rule stores the fleet's expectations under that number: the vehicles it's waiting for, and a map for what's received.
- In the postlude it raises `report:scatter` to start the work and schedules `report:timer_expired`, both carrying the number.

Any rule that sees an `rcn` must pass it on. Future versions of Wrangler may automate more of this.

### Event recipient lists

The simplest routing is to keep a list of picos and send the same event to each of them, like the **To:** line of an email. The list can be fixed, or computed, so that the pico acts as an event router. Here the list is the fleet's current children:

```krl
// 2. Scatter: one event per vehicle, from a computed recipient list.
rule scatter {
  select when report scatter
  foreach vehicles() setting(vehicle)
  event:send({
    "eci": vehicle{"eci"},
    "domain": "report",
    "type": "vehicle_report_requested",
    "attrs": {"rcn": event:attr("rcn")}
  })
}
```

- `foreach` runs the rest of the rule once for each vehicle that `vehicles()` returns, setting `vehicle` each time. If vehicles are added or removed, the next report just uses the new list.
- `event:send` goes in the action block. It sends `report:vehicle_report_requested` over the family channel to each vehicle.
- The number goes along with it.

The vehicle pico does its part, and it can take as long as it likes:

```krl
ruleset com.example.vehicle {
  meta {
    name "Vehicle"
    use module io.picolabs.wrangler alias wrangler
    shares summary
  }
  global {
    /**
     * What this vehicle has done.
     * @returns Map
     */
    summary = function() {
      {"trips": ent:trips.defaultsTo(0), "miles": ent:miles.defaultsTo(0)}
    }
  }

  rule produce_vehicle_report {
    select when report vehicle_report_requested rcn re#(.+)# setting(rcn)
    event:send({
      "eci": wrangler:parent_eci(),
      "domain": "report",
      "type": "vehicle_report_created",
      "attrs": {"rcn": rcn, "vehicle": wrangler:name(), "details": summary()}
    })
  }
}
```

It sends the answer to its parent with the number and its name, so the fleet can tell who replied.

### Aggregators

An **aggregator** collects events and, when it has enough, raises an event or takes another action. The fleet's is two rules: one collects, and one decides.

```krl
// 3. Gather: file each answer under its correlation number.
rule catch_vehicle_report {
  select when report vehicle_report_created
  pre {
    rcn = event:attr("rcn")
    open = reports() >< rcn
  }
  if open then noop()
  fired {
    ent:reports{[rcn, "received", event:attr("vehicle")]} := event:attr("details")
    raise report event "vehicle_report_added" attributes {"rcn": rcn}
  }
}
```

- The rule files the vehicle's details under `[rcn, "received", vehicle name]`, so overlapping reports can't interfere, and a vehicle that answers twice just overwrites itself.
- The rule only acts if the report is still open (`reports() >< rcn`). An answer that arrives after the report has finished is ignored.
- It raises `report:vehicle_report_added` with the number so another rule can decide.

```krl
// 4. Check: is everyone in?
rule check_report_status {
  select when report vehicle_report_added
  pre {
    rcn = event:attr("rcn")
    report = ent:reports{rcn}
    still_waiting = report{"expected"}.defaultsTo([]).difference(report{"received"}.defaultsTo({}).keys())
  }
  if not report.isnull() && still_waiting.length() == 0 then noop()
  fired {
    raise report event "ready" attributes {"rcn": rcn}
  }
}
```

- The prelude works out which expected vehicles haven't answered. Each is in `expected` but not among the keys of `received`.
- If none is missing, the rule fires and raises `report:ready`. Otherwise it does nothing: there's no waiting, no loop, and the next answer will run this rule again.

### Dealing with failure

The timer was scheduled when the report began. When it expires, the rule sees whether the report is still open, and if it is, raises the same `report:ready` event, marked `timed_out`:

```krl
// The timer is a safety net, not the way the work normally finishes.
rule timer_expired {
  select when report timer_expired
  pre {
    rcn = event:attr("rcn")
  }
  if reports() >< rcn then noop()
  fired {
    raise report event "ready" attributes {"rcn": rcn, "timed_out": true}
  }
}
```

Whichever comes first, the last answer or the timer, ends in `report:ready`. The rule that finishes the report has to make sure it only does so once:

```krl
// 5. Finish once, however we got here.
rule finish_report {
  select when report ready
  pre {
    rcn = event:attr("rcn")
    report = ent:reports{rcn}
    missing = report{"expected"}.defaultsTo([]).difference(report{"received"}.defaultsTo({}).keys())
  }
  if not report.isnull() then noop()
  fired {
    ent:completed{rcn} := {
      "details": report{"received"},
      "missing": missing,
      "time": time:now()
    }
    clear ent:reports{rcn}
  }
}
```

It runs only if `ent:reports{rcn}` still exists, and it clears it. So a late answer, or a timer that expires after the report is done, finds nothing to do. The finished report lists the `details` it has and which vehicles are `missing`, so a reader knows what it's made of.

To retry instead of just continuing, have `timer_expired` raise `report:scatter` again for only the missing vehicles (the same `rcn`), count the attempts, schedule the timer again, and finish after the limit. Fuse did this: up to two retries, two minutes apart, and then a report with what it had.

### Content-based event routing

Another way to decide who gets an event is by what it says. The routing pico knows several others and chooses by the event's domain, type, attributes, or its own state. A Fuse fleet could have more than one owner and needed to keep an owner informed by routing certain events to one:

```krl
// Content-based routing: the event decides where it goes.
rule route_to_owner {
  select when fleet new_trip
           or fleet reminders_ready
           or fleet email_for_owner
  pre {
    owner = relationship:established("Tx_role", "owner").head()
  }
  if owner then
    event:send({
      "sub": owner,
      "domain": "fleet",
      "type": event:type(),
      "attrs": event:attrs
    })
}
```

- The event expression says which events get routed. It's fixed when the rule is written. To route on something computed, chain rules.
- `relationship:established("Tx_role", "owner")` finds the relationships whose other end is an owner. `head()` takes the first. To tell every owner, loop over them with `foreach`.
- `event:send` with `"sub"` sends over the relationship. The type and attributes of the incoming event go along unchanged.

### Registration

The most general routing is a directory. Picos send a registration event saying who they are and what they care about, and the directory routes events to those that have registered for them. The directory can be a special pico in a large system, or a ruleset in a pico that does other things too. A directory also lets a pico change its channel for security without losing service, and lets a pico move without losing messages.

```krl
// Registration: picos say what they want to hear about.
rule register_pico {
  select when registry pico_registered
    topic re#(.+)#
    eci re#(.+)#
    setting(topic, eci)
  always {
    ent:registrations{[topic, eci]} := event:attr("name")
  }
}
```

```krl
rule route_to_registered {
  select when fleet events_to_route
           or fleet another_event_to_route
  foreach registered(event:attr("topic")) setting(eci)
  event:send({
    "eci": eci,
    "domain": "fleet",
    "type": event:type(),
    "attrs": event:attrs
  })
}
```

The first rule files each registrant under its topic. The second sends an incoming event to every pico registered for the event's `topic`. A registrar goes a step further: it manages the registry on behalf of the picos, watching `wrangler:child_initialized` and `wrangler:child_deleted` and registering and deregistering as they come and go. The picos needn't know the registry exists.

## Try it

Make a fleet pico with two or three children. Install `com.example.vehicle` in each child, and `com.example.fleet` in the parent. The easy way is to use the chain from [Pico-Based Systems](/lessons/pico-based-systems): `new_child_request`, then `child_initialized`, then `install_ruleset_request`.

On the fleet's Testing tab, raise `report:requested`. Query `completed` and you'll see one report with every vehicle's details, an empty `missing` list, and the correlation number as its key. Then try it the hard way:

- Uninstall `com.example.vehicle` from one child and raise `report:requested` again. The report completes after the timer expires, with that vehicle in `missing`.
- Raise `report:requested` twice quickly. There are two numbers and two independent reports.

## Conclusion

Scatter-gather adds a few rules over the synchronous version, and each is short and does one thing. What you get for it:

- **Reliability.** The synchronous version fails when any vehicle is slow. This one finishes even when one is dead.
- **Better use of the fleet pico.** It doesn't sit waiting. It handles other events while the vehicles work, and takes the answers as they arrive.
- **No locks.** The fleet pico may get answers from many vehicles at once, but they queue and are handled one at a time. Because each pico is independent, concurrent processing needs no locks, inside a pico or between picos. This is a property of actor systems, and picos are actors.

Vernon's book is a good companion. Its language and framework (Scala and Akka) are different, but the concepts carry over directly to picos.

## Related

- [Child pico tasks](/cookbook/child_tasks/): a pico per job, with a task id and no waiting
- [Querying another pico](/developing/querying-another-pico): when a synchronous query is the right tool
- [Relationships](/wrangler/relationships) and [The wrangler ruleset](/wrangler/wrangler): the events and functions used here
- [Gossip](/lessons/gossip): an advanced lab in which picos exchange state by events

# Lesson: Gossip Lab

# Gossip Lab

The Gossip Lab is an optional, advanced exercise. It was the ninth lab (Lab 9) in BYU CS 462, the course that uses picos to teach reactive, event-based programming. The Pico Programming Lessons list it last, and it isn't part of the main sequence.

## What's here, and what isn't

The original wiki page is almost empty. It holds one thing: a video recorded for the Lab 9 assignment. You can watch it on YouTube: [Gossip Lab video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WrBf9kg-_ZY).

This engine's documentation doesn't reproduce the assignment. The wiki page doesn't contain it (students got the assignment through the course), and rather than guess at the protocol, this page stops here. If you're taking the course, use the assignment text from your instructor.

## Preparing for it

Whatever the details of the assignment, a gossip-style system of picos uses things these lessons teach. If you want to be ready, work through:

- [Pico-Based Systems](/lessons/pico-based-systems): create a set of picos and keep track of them
- [Relationships](/lessons/relationships): link picos that aren't parent and child, and send events over the link
- [Scatter-Gather](/lessons/scatter-gather): send events to many picos without waiting, correlate the answers, and deal with lost events
- [Pico State](/lessons/pico-state): keep and update persistent state

In the cookbook, [Two picos talking](/cookbook/two_picos/) and [Collection](/cookbook/collection/) are small runnable examples of picos with relationships. Picos communicate only by events and queries, so any distributed protocol on picos is built from those, plus a channel policy for what each peer may do.

## Back to the lessons

The main sequence starts at the [Quickstart](/lessons/quickstart).

# Cookbook

# Cookbook

Worked examples you can install and run. Each recipe has an overview and step-by-step instructions. The KRL lives in the pico-engine repository under [`demos/`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/tree/master/demos), and the engine ships a copy.

The quickest start is the **Try It!** tab on the root pico in the developer UI (engine config `show_tryit_menu` can show it on every pico, or hide it). It lists the demos that have a bootstrap ruleset. Open one and **Run** it: the tab creates a child pico and installs that ruleset, which sets up the whole demo. The same window shows each ruleset's code and its path on disk. Edit a file, **Flush**, and watch the demo change. Agents can do the same with the dev MCP server (`pico-engine mcp --stdio`): `list_try_it_demos`, `run_try_it_demo`, and `try_it_status`. It also serves these pages as `pico://docs/cookbook/...` resources.

The demos are meant for an engine without [OAuth](/pico-views?id=oauth-protected-meshes), such as one on your own machine. On a mesh with OAuth turned on they still install, but their pages and `curl` examples call the pico without an access token, so they may not load their data. The Try It! tab says so when that's the case.

| Recipe | What it shows | KRL |
|--------|---------------|-----|
| [Echo](/cookbook/echo/) | The hello world of events: a rule answers an event with a directive, from a page or from `curl` | [`demos/echo/`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/tree/master/demos/echo) |
| [Score tracker](/cookbook/score_tracker/) | A contest pico with a leaderboard, and an app channel whose policy lets contestants play without changing the pico | [`demos/score_tracker/`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/tree/master/demos/score_tracker) |
| [Pico views](/cookbook/xmlui/) | XMLUI pages served from a pico: queries, events, app channels, detail routes, components (the Thermostat demo), and a view over another pico's data | [`demos/xmlui/`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/tree/master/demos/xmlui) |
| [Two picos talking](/cookbook/two_picos/) | Two picos form a relationship, and one queries the other over it | [`demos/two_picos/`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/tree/master/demos/two_picos) |
| [Child pico tasks](/cookbook/child_tasks/) | Running each task in a new child pico that reports back and deletes itself, so the parent never waits | [`demos/child_tasks/`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/tree/master/demos/child_tasks) |
| [Guard rules](/cookbook/guard_rules/) | Making a request idempotent with a guard rule, and refusing work with a gate rule and `last` until it can be done | [`demos/guard_rules/`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/tree/master/demos/guard_rules) |
| [Layered rulesets](/cookbook/layered_rulesets/) | Rules that each do one thing and raise an event, and add-on rulesets that change what a pico does without editing the base | [`demos/layered_rulesets/`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/tree/master/demos/layered_rulesets) |
| [Collection](/cookbook/collection/) | A pico that keeps a collection of other picos over relationships, accepts members by role, and reports on all of them | [`demos/collection/`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/tree/master/demos/collection) |
| [Configuration and secrets](/cookbook/secrets/) | Getting a secret into a ruleset with install configuration or an event, keeping a ruleset idle until it has one, and where secrets stay visible | [`demos/secrets/`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/tree/master/demos/secrets) |
| [Bootstrap and channels](/cookbook/bootstrap/) | A bootstrap ruleset installing an app in dependency order with configuration, and an app that creates or updates its own channel on install, with a policy built from its schema | [`demos/bootstrap/`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/tree/master/demos/bootstrap) |
| [KBlog](/cookbook/kblog/) | A blog written in KRL: four rulesets that work together through an event hierarchy, with a reader channel and an author channel | [`demos/kblog/`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/tree/master/demos/kblog) |
| [Querying JSON](/cookbook/json_query/) | Finding values in nested JSON with the `query()` operator and JSONPath: four canned queries over a fleet's data, or your own | [`demos/json_query/`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/tree/master/demos/json_query) |
| [Moving picos](/cookbook/moving_picos/) | Exporting a pico and its children from one engine and importing them on another, keeping its did:webvh identity and relationships | [`demos/moving_picos/`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/tree/master/demos/moving_picos) |


---

# Cookbook: pico views

# Pico views

Seven small rulesets that serve [XMLUI](https://xmlui.org) pages from a pico. Each one adds one idea, from a static page to a view that shows another pico's data. They are also the test fixtures for the engine's view routes.

Read [Pico views](/pico-views) for how views work. To install and open these, follow the [instructions](/cookbook/xmlui/instructions).

## The rulesets

| Ruleset | File | What it shows |
|---------|------|---------------|
| Hello | [`com.example.hello.krl`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/blob/master/demos/xmlui/com.example.hello.krl) | A `@view` function and nothing else |
| Favorite color | [`com.example.fav_color.krl`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/blob/master/demos/xmlui/com.example.fav_color.krl) | Reading with `ui:query` and writing with `ui:event`, then refreshing |
| Guestbook | [`com.example.guestbook.krl`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/blob/master/demos/xmlui/com.example.guestbook.krl) | An app channel created on install with `ui:create_app_channel` |
| Contacts | [`com.example.contacts.krl`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/blob/master/demos/xmlui/com.example.contacts.krl) | A list page and a detail page (`/contact/:id`), seeded with two contacts |
| Thermostat | [`com.example.thermostat.krl`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/blob/master/demos/xmlui/com.example.thermostat.krl) | Two channels with different policies (viewer and admin), an app `@component`, and the shared `PicoSettings`, `PicoThemeField`, and `PicoTheme` components |
| Thermostat bootstrap | [`com.example.thermostat.bootstrap.krl`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/blob/master/demos/xmlui/com.example.thermostat.bootstrap.krl) | Sets up the whole Thermostat demo on a new pico. The developer UI's **Try It!** tab runs it |
| Temperature sensors (data) | [`temperature_sensors.krl`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/blob/master/demos/xmlui/temperature_sensors.krl) | Sample readings on a data pico |
| Temperature sensors (view) | [`com.example.temperature_sensors_view.krl`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/blob/master/demos/xmlui/com.example.temperature_sensors_view.krl) | A view on one pico over data on another, reached through a relationship |

## What you need

- A running pico engine. Components (`@component` and the shared `Pico*` components, used by Thermostat) need pico-engine 1.9.4 or later.
- `io.picolabs.xmlui` installed on each pico that serves a view. The engine ships it at `/krl/io.picolabs.xmlui.krl` but does not install it anywhere by default.
