- **Posting** (`com.example.kblog.posting`): checks each post an author submits and passes it on.
- **Configuration** (`com.example.kblog.config`): the title and the fixed text.

Readers and authors use different channels on the same pico. The reader channel opens every page except Post and accepts no events. The author channel, which the posting ruleset creates when it is installed, adds the Post page and exactly two events. Each time an author posts, the Post page shows the path the post took through the rulesets.

To run it, follow the [instructions](/cookbook/kblog/instructions).

## The event hierarchy

Events are nouns: they say what happened. Rules are verbs: they say what the pico does about it. The write side of KBlog is a chain of them:

```
kblog:post_submitted                      (from the author channel)
  ├─ handle_submit      posting  ──▶  kblog:new_article_available
  │                                     └─ add_article        data   ──▶  kblog:new_article_added
  │                                                                         └─ show_new_article  pages  ──▶  kblog:front_page_updated
  └─ reject_submit      posting       (no name or title: nothing is added)

kblog:clear_requested                     (from the author channel)
  └─ clear_articles     data     ──▶  kblog:articles_cleared
                                        └─ show_empty_blog    pages  ──▶  kblog:front_page_updated
```

Every rule that changes something raises an event saying what is now true, even when nothing listens yet (`front_page_updated`). A ruleset added later can react without anyone editing these.

The read side is queries, not events. The Home page calls `articles()` and an article page calls `article(id)`, which the pages ruleset gets from the data ruleset as a module.

## From the 2011 KBlog

The [original KBlog](https://github.com/windley/KBlog) ran on the classic engine, which raised events from a browser and let rules paint the page. Its design is described in [Event Hierarchies: A Blog Written in KRL](https://www.windley.com/archives/2011/04/event_hierarchies_a_blog_written_in_krl.shtml). This version keeps its rulesets, rule names, and events where they still make sense:

| 2011 | Now |
|------|-----|
| KBlog (`a16x88`) painted the page with `replace_html` in response to `pageview` and `web:click` | `com.example.kblog` serves XMLUI pages. Navigation and the back button come from the page routes (`/`, `/post/:id`, `/contact`, `/new`) |
| `show_home` raised `need_blog_data`; KBlog Data answered with `blog_data_ready` carrying the articles | The page queries `articles()`. Reading is a query; writing stays a chain of events |
| KBlog Data (`a16x89`) kept the articles in an application variable | `com.example.kblog.data` keeps them in an entity variable on the blog pico. `add_article` and `new_article_added` are unchanged |
| KBlog Posting (`a16x90`) ran only for people who had installed it in their browser | `com.example.kblog.posting` creates the author channel. The channel's policy, not who has the code, decides who can post |
| KBlog Configuration (`a16x93`) provided the title, about text, and shared actions | `com.example.kblog.config` provides the title and text. The page layout is a component (`BlogAbout`) |
| KBlog Tweeter (`a16x91`) tweeted new posts | Left out. A ruleset that selects `kblog:new_article_added` would be its place |

## The rulesets

| Ruleset | File | What it shows |
|---------|------|---------------|
| Pages | [`com.example.kblog.krl`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/blob/master/demos/kblog/com.example.kblog.krl) | Four `@view`s with routes, including a detail page (`/post/:id`); a `@component` used on every page; Markdown rendered safely from data; a page whose form comes from another ruleset; the reader channel |
| Data | [`com.example.kblog.data.krl`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/blob/master/demos/kblog/com.example.kblog.data.krl) | One ruleset owning the data: rules that change it raise events, and `provides` lets other rulesets read it |
| Posting | [`com.example.kblog.posting.krl`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/blob/master/demos/kblog/com.example.kblog.posting.krl) | Checking input before raising the internal event; a `@component` another ruleset's page shows; a channel policy that names single events |
| Configuration | [`com.example.kblog.config.krl`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/blob/master/demos/kblog/com.example.kblog.config.krl) | A module of settings other rulesets use |
| Bootstrap | [`com.example.kblog.bootstrap.krl`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/blob/master/demos/kblog/com.example.kblog.bootstrap.krl) | Installing rulesets in dependency order, each on the previous one's `ruleset_installed`, then submitting three posts. The developer UI's **Try It!** tab runs it |

## What you need

- A running pico engine (1.9.4 or later: the pages use components).
- `io.picolabs.xmlui` on the blog pico. The bootstrap installs it.


---

# Cookbook: KBlog instructions

# KBlog: instructions

These steps use the developer UI of a running engine at `http://localhost:3000`. Replace that with your engine's URL. See the [overview](/cookbook/kblog/) for what the demo shows and how it differs from the 2011 KBlog.

## The quick way: Try It!

On the root pico in the developer UI, open the **Try It!** tab, click **KBlog**, then **Run in a new child pico**. The bootstrap installs the rulesets and submits three posts. When it shows **ready**, it has two links:

- **Read the blog (reader channel)**: Home and Contact. There is no Post page.
- **Write a post (author channel)**: Home, Contact, and Post.

## By hand

1. Create a child pico and open its **Rulesets** tab.
2. Install these from the engine, in this order. Each one after the first uses an earlier one as a module.
   - `http://localhost:3000/krl/io.picolabs.xmlui.krl`
   - `http://localhost:3000/krl/demos/kblog/com.example.kblog.config.krl`
   - `http://localhost:3000/krl/demos/kblog/com.example.kblog.data.krl`
   - `http://localhost:3000/krl/demos/kblog/com.example.kblog.krl`, which creates the `kblog, reader` channel
   - `http://localhost:3000/krl/demos/kblog/com.example.kblog.posting.krl`, which creates the `kblog, author` channel
3. Click **View** next to `com.example.kblog` and open it on either channel.

## Try it

- On the author channel, open **Post**, write a post, and click **Post**. The **Event path** card reads `handle_submit → add_article → show_new_article`: one rule in each of three rulesets. Open **Home**: your post is first, marked **New**.
- Submit a post without a title. The path is `reject_submit`, and nothing is added.
- Click an article's title. Its page is at `#/post/<id>`, so you can bookmark it, and the browser's back button returns to Home.
- On the reader channel, try to post anyway. Replace `<reader eci>` with the id in the reader page's URL:

  ```sh
  curl -X POST "http://localhost:3000/sky/event/<reader eci>/demo/kblog/post_submitted" \
    -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"author": "Mallory", "title": "Hi"}'
  ```

  The answer is `{"error":"Error: Not allowed by channel policy"}`.
- On the author channel, try to skip the check by raising the internal event yourself: `kblog/new_article_available` instead of `kblog/post_submitted`. The author channel refuses it too. It allows `post_submitted` and `clear_requested` and nothing else.
- **Clear the blog** on the Post page deletes every article. The path is `clear_articles → show_empty_blog`.

## How it works

**Posting** checks a post and passes it on. It doesn't store anything:

```krl
rule handle_submit {
  select when kblog post_submitted
    author re#(\S.*)#
    title re#(\S.*)#
    setting(author, title)
  send_directive("handle_submit", {"title": title})
  fired {
    raise kblog event "new_article_available" attributes
      {"author": author, "title": title, "body": event:attr("body") || ""}
  }
}
```

**Data** stores the article and says so:

```krl
rule add_article {
  select when kblog new_article_available
  pre {
    id = ent:next_id.defaultsTo(1)
    entry = {"id": id, "author": event:attr("author"), "title": event:attr("title"),
             "body": event:attr("body") || "", "time": time:now()}
  }
  send_directive("add_article", {"id": id})
  fired {
    ent:next_id := id + 1
    ent:articles{id.as("String")} := entry
    raise kblog event "new_article_added" attributes entry
  }
}
```

**Pages** marks the newest article and raises `kblog:front_page_updated`. The Home page reloads its articles every five seconds, so readers see new posts without reloading.

Each rule answers with a directive named after itself. A raised event is handled in the same transaction as the event that raised it, after that event's rules finish. So the response to `post_submitted` holds the directives of every rule that ran, in order. The Post page joins their names into the event path.

**Who can post** is the author channel's policy:

```krl
wrangler:createChannel(
  ["kblog", "author"],
  {"allow": [{"domain": "kblog", "name": "post_submitted"}, {"domain": "kblog", "name": "clear_requested"}], "deny": []},
  authorQueryPolicy()
)
```

Its query policy allows every page, including Post, plus the posting ruleset's `PostForm` component. The reader channel, made by `ui:create_app_channel` in the pages ruleset, allows the other pages and no events. The navigation shows only the pages a channel allows, so readers never see Post.

**The Post page** is in the pages ruleset, but its form is the `PostForm` component from the posting ruleset. The engine finds a component in the app's ruleset, then in `io.picolabs.xmlui`, then in one other installed ruleset that defines it.

**Article text** is Markdown from whoever posted it, so the pages render it with `<Markdown content="{$item.body}" allowHtml="false" interpolateBindings="false" />`. HTML in a post shows as text, and nothing in it is evaluated.

## Change it and watch

The **Try It!** window lists each file with its path on disk. Edit a file there, click **Flush**, and reload the page.

- Rename the blog: change the string `blogtitle` returns in `com.example.kblog.config.krl`, flush it, and reload. The pages call the configuration module each time they are generated, so only the module needs flushing.
- Put back the tweeter as a new ruleset whose rule selects `kblog:new_article_added`, records each title, and sends a directive named after itself. Install it from a `file://` URL and post: the event path gets a fourth name, with no change to the other rulesets.
- Add a word limit: a rule in `com.example.kblog.posting.krl` that rejects bodies over 200 words. Make `handle_submit` skip them too, so only one of the two rules runs.


---

# Cookbook: querying JSON

# Querying JSON

Picos often hold large, nested data: API responses, sensor histories, a fleet's trips and fill-ups. KRL's [`query()`](/krl/krl-expression-language/operators/query-operator) operator finds values in that data with a [JSONPath](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9535) expression, instead of a chain of `get()`, `map()`, and `filter()` calls.

This demo's pico holds the vehicles, trips, and fill-ups of a small fleet, the kind of data Fuse, a pico-based connected-car platform, kept for each vehicle. Its page shows the data and runs four queries against it, each showing a different part of JSONPath. You can also type your own.

| Query | Path | Shows |
|-------|------|-------|
| Every vehicle's name | `$.vehicles[*].name` | Child selectors and the wildcard |
| All the miles, at any depth | `$..miles` | The descendant selector |
| Business trips over 25 miles | `$.vehicles[*].trips[?@.category == 'business' && @.miles > 25]` | A filter with two tests |
| Each vehicle's latest fill-up | `$.vehicles[?count(@.fillups[*]) > 0].fillups[-1]` | A filter function and a negative index |

To run it, follow the [instructions](/cookbook/json_query/instructions).

## The rulesets

| Ruleset | File | What it shows |
|---------|------|---------------|
| Querying JSON | [`com.example.json_query.krl`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/blob/master/demos/json_query/com.example.json_query.krl) | The data as a global map, `query()` in a shared function, and a `@view` that sends the path as a query parameter and shows the results. Creates an app channel that allows the page's queries and no events |
| Querying JSON bootstrap | [`com.example.json_query.bootstrap.krl`](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/blob/master/demos/json_query/com.example.json_query.bootstrap.krl) | Sets up the demo on a new pico. The developer UI's **Try It!** tab runs it |

## What you need

- A running pico engine with the `query()` operator (after 1.9.5).
- `io.picolabs.xmlui` on the pico for the page. The bootstrap installs it.


---

# Cookbook: querying JSON instructions

# Querying JSON: instructions

These steps use the developer UI of a running engine at `http://localhost:3000`. Replace that with your engine's URL. See the [overview](/cookbook/json_query/) for what the demo shows.

## The quick way: Try It!

On the root pico in the developer UI, open the **Try It!** tab, click **Querying JSON**, then **Run in a new child pico**. When it shows **ready**, open **Query page**.

## By hand

1. Create a child pico and open its **Rulesets** tab.
2. Install `io.picolabs.xmlui` from the engine: `http://localhost:3000/krl/io.picolabs.xmlui.krl`.
3. Install the demo ruleset: `http://localhost:3000/krl/demos/json_query/com.example.json_query.krl`.
4. Installing it creates a channel tagged `json_query, app`. Click **View** next to `com.example.json_query` and open it on that channel.

## Try it

- Click **Show the JSON**. The fleet data appears beside the queries.
- Click each query button. The card shows the path, what it uses, and the values `query()` found.
- Type your own path and click **Run it**:
  - `$.owner.email`: one value, still in an array
  - `$.vehicles[?@.year > 2020].name`: a filter on a number
  - `$..cost`: every trip's cost
  - `$.vehicles[0].trips[-1:]`: the last trip of the first vehicle, as a slice
  - `$.vehicles[?match(@.make, 'T.*')].model`: a regular expression
  - `$.nope`: no match, an empty array
- Type a broken path such as `$.vehicles[?@.year >`. The pico answers with the parse error.
- Run a query from a terminal. The path has to be URL-encoded:

  ```sh
  curl "http://localhost:3000/sky/query/<eci>/com.example.json_query/runQuery?path=%24..miles"
  ```

## How it works

The data is a map in the ruleset's `global` block, and one shared function queries it:

```krl
runQuery = function(path) {
  result = fleet.query(path)
  answer = {"path": path, "count": result.length(), "result": result}
  answer
}
```

`query()` always returns an array, even for one match, and an empty array when nothing matches. An invalid path is an error, which the engine returns to the page as `{"error": …}`.

The page fetches `runQuery` with a `DataSource` whose `queryParams` send the path. `DataSource` URL-encodes it, which matters because JSONPath uses `$`, `?`, `&&`, and quotes:

```xml
<DataSource id="run" url="#{run_url}" headers="{appGlobals.auth}" queryParams="{{path: path}}" when="{path}" />
```

Each button sets `path`, and the `DataSource` fetches again whenever `path` changes. The canned queries come from another shared function, `cannedQueries()`, so the page doesn't have to put JSONPath strings in XML attributes.

The JSON is shown with `JSON.stringify(value, null, 2)` in a `Text` with `variant="mono"` and `preserveLinebreaks`.

## Change it and watch

The **Try It!** window lists each file with its path on disk. Edit `com.example.json_query.krl` there, click **Flush**, and reload the page.

- Add a fifth entry to `cannedQueries()`, for example the total of fuel bought: `$.vehicles[*].fillups[*].gallons`. Then sum the result in KRL with `.reduce(function(a, b) { a + b }, 0)`.
- Add a vehicle to `fleet`, and run the queries again.
- Write a function that uses `query()` for something useful, such as the business miles of one vehicle: `fleet.query("$.vehicles[?@.name == '" + name + "'].trips[?@.category == 'business'].miles")`. See the [`query()` page](/krl/krl-expression-language/operators/query-operator) on checking values before putting them in a path.


---

# Wrangler: the pico operating system

# Wrangler

Wrangler is the operating system for picos. The engine itself provides primitives: picos, channels, events, queries, persistence, identity. Wrangler is a set of KRL rulesets, installed on every pico, that wraps those primitives in events and functions your rulesets use: create and delete child picos, install rulesets, make channels, form relationships with other picos, and keep a pico's profile and data.

Use Wrangler rather than the engine's `ctx:` primitives from application rulesets. Wrangler is the supported API for a pico's life cycle. If something you need isn't there, treat it as out of bounds, or [file an engine issue](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/issues).

## The rulesets on every pico

The engine installs these on the root pico, and Wrangler installs them on every child it creates:

| Ruleset | What it does | Guide | API reference |
|---------|--------------|-------|---------------|
| `io.picolabs.wrangler` | A pico's life cycle: child picos, rulesets, channels, and queries to other picos | [The wrangler ruleset](/wrangler/wrangler) | [io.picolabs.wrangler](/rulesets/io.picolabs.wrangler) |
| `io.picolabs.subscription` | Relationships between picos (called subscriptions before engine 1.6.2) | [Relationships](/wrangler/relationships) | [io.picolabs.subscription](/rulesets/io.picolabs.subscription) |
| `io.picolabs.pds` | The pico's profile and its shared, namespaced data | [Pico data store](/wrangler/pds) | [io.picolabs.pds](/rulesets/io.picolabs.pds) |
| `io.picolabs.pico-engine-ui` | What the developer UI needs: its channel, the pico's box, Testing tab history | — | [io.picolabs.pico-engine-ui](/rulesets/io.picolabs.pico-engine-ui) |

Channels are the engine's, but Wrangler is how rulesets manage them: see [Managing channels](/wrangler/channels).

## Optional rulesets

The engine ships these too, at `/krl/<rid>.krl`, but doesn't install them. Install one from a pico's **Rulesets** tab, or with `wrangler:install_ruleset_request`, when you need it:

| Ruleset | What it does | Guide |
|---------|--------------|-------|
| `io.picolabs.xmlui` | Pages served from a pico (pico views) and the components they share | [Pico views](/wrangler/xmlui) |
| `io.picolabs.oauth` | Root pico only: require OAuth access tokens on the mesh's `/sky/*` traffic, and manage OAuth credentials | [OAuth](/wrangler/oauth) |
| `io.picolabs.portable_subtree` | Export a pico and its children, and import them under another parent, on this engine or another | [Portable subtrees](/wrangler/portable-subtree) |

## Using Wrangler from a ruleset

Each Wrangler ruleset works two ways:

- **Events.** Raise or send an event that a Wrangler rule selects, such as `wrangler:new_child_request` or `wrangler:install_ruleset_request`. When the work is done, Wrangler raises an event saying so, such as `wrangler:child_initialized` or `wrangler:ruleset_installed`, which your rules can select.
- **Functions and actions.** Use the ruleset as a module and call what it provides:

  ```krl
  meta {
    use module io.picolabs.wrangler alias wrangler
  }
  ```

  Then `wrangler:children()`, `wrangler:channels(["myapp", "app"])`, `wrangler:createChannel(...)`, and so on. Shared functions can also be queried from outside the pico, on a channel whose policy allows them.

The guides explain how the pieces fit together. The API reference pages list every event and function each ruleset supports, generated from the rulesets' own doc comments.

Wrangler and the engine know nothing about any particular application. Frameworks such as Manifold build on Wrangler to give a mesh of picos its own vocabulary.


---

# Wrangler: the wrangler ruleset

# The wrangler ruleset

`io.picolabs.wrangler` manages a pico's life cycle: its child picos, the rulesets installed in it, and its channels. It also has the functions rulesets use to learn about the pico and to query other picos. For every event and function, see the [API reference](/rulesets/io.picolabs.wrangler). For what Wrangler is as a whole, see [Wrangler](/wrangler/).

The examples assume the ruleset uses Wrangler as a module:

```krl
meta {
  use module io.picolabs.wrangler alias wrangler
}
```

## Pico life cycle

The engine creates the first pico, the root pico, when it starts for the first time. Any pico can create child picos, and a pico can delete its children. The root pico can't be deleted.

### Creating a child pico

Raise `wrangler:new_child_request` in the pico that will be the parent, with a `name` and, optionally, a `backgroundColor` for the developer UI:

```krl
raise wrangler event "new_child_request" attributes {"name": "Kitchen", "task_id": "42"}
```

Wrangler's `createChild` rule creates the child pico with the developer UI ruleset and Wrangler installed, then sends the child three events in order:

1. `engine_ui:setup`: the developer UI ruleset creates the channel the UI uses for this pico.
2. `wrangler:pico_created`: Wrangler on the child records its name, parent, and id, and installs `io.picolabs.pds` and `io.picolabs.subscription`.
3. `engine_ui:box`: the UI ruleset stores the name and color the developer UI shows.

Then, in the parent, Wrangler raises `wrangler:new_child_created`, with the child's family channel (`eci`) and its UI channel (`uiEci`). When the child has finished setting up, it raises `wrangler:pico_initialized` for itself and sends `wrangler:child_initialized` to its parent.

Any other attributes on the request (`task_id` above) are passed through: they arrive on the child with `pico_created`, and come back to the parent with `new_child_created` and `child_initialized`. That's how a parent tells its new children apart. The parent selects `child_initialized` with a `where` on its own attribute, and gets the child's `eci` to send it more events, such as an `install_ruleset_request`. See the [Child pico tasks](/cookbook/child_tasks/) demo.

`new_child_request` also takes an optional `policyCeiling`: a map that limits the channel policies the child may ever have. It can't exceed the parent's own ceiling.

The developer UI's **About** tab creates children the same way: it sends `engine_ui:new`, which raises `wrangler:new_child_request`.

### While a pico exists

| Function | Returns |
|----------|---------|
| `parent_eci()` | The family channel this pico uses to reach its parent. `null` on the root pico |
| `children()` | An array of maps, one per child: `{"eci": ..., "name": ..., "parent_eci": ...}`. `eci` is this pico's family channel to the child |
| `myself()` | `{"name": ..., "id": ..., "eci": ...}` for this pico |
| `name()`, `id()` | This pico's name and id |
| `myDid()`, `publicIntro()` | This pico's portable `did:webvh`, and whether it accepts introductions on it. See [Relationships](/wrangler/relationships) |

`wrangler:name_changed` with a `name` changes the pico's name.

### Deleting a pico

A pico can only be deleted by its parent. A rule in the parent raises `wrangler:child_deletion_request` with `eci` set to the child's family channel, from `children()`:

```krl
raise wrangler event "child_deletion_request" attributes {"eci": child{"eci"}}
```

The child and all its descendants are deleted, and Wrangler raises `wrangler:child_deleted` in the parent with the same attributes.

A pico can ask to be deleted by raising `wrangler:ready_for_deletion`. Wrangler sends its parent the `child_deletion_request` for it. Finish any work in progress and release what the pico holds first.

There's no undo. When a pico is deleted, its state, channels, and relationships are gone.

The root pico can't be deleted. The only way to remove every pico, the root included, is to stop the engine and remove its database, `db/` in the engine's home directory (`~/.pico-engine` by default). That also removes passkey registrations and every pico's identity. The next start creates a new root pico, and the first visit registers a new passkey. Use it only as a last resort.

### Life cycle events

Events Wrangler selects:

| Event | Sent by | Attributes |
|-------|---------|------------|
| `wrangler:new_child_request` | The developer UI or a ruleset | `name`; optional `backgroundColor`, `policyCeiling`, and any others to pass through |
| `wrangler:pico_created` | Wrangler, to the new child (not for rulesets) | Those of the request |
| `wrangler:child_deletion_request` | The developer UI, a ruleset, or Wrangler on a child | `eci`, the family channel to the child |
| `wrangler:ready_for_deletion` | A ruleset on the pico to delete | None |
| `wrangler:name_changed` | A ruleset | `name` |

Events Wrangler raises:

| Event | Where | Attributes |
|-------|-------|------------|
| `wrangler:new_child_created` | In the parent | Those of the request, plus the child's `eci` and `uiEci` |
| `wrangler:pico_initialized` | In the child | Those of the request, plus the child's `eci` |
| `wrangler:child_initialized` | Sent from the child to the parent | Those of the request, plus `eci` |
| `wrangler:child_deleted` | In the parent | Those of the deletion request |

## Channels

A pico can have as many channels as it needs, and only a pico can create and delete its own. Channels and their policies are explained in [Managing channels](/wrangler/channels). This section is the Wrangler API for them.

### Creating a channel

`createChannel(tags, eventPolicy, queryPolicy)` is an action that creates a channel and returns it. Its `id` is the channel's ECI:

```krl
rule initialize {
  select when wrangler ruleset_installed where event:attr("rids") >< meta:rid
  if ent:app_eci.isnull() then
    wrangler:createChannel(
      ["myapp", "app"],
      {"allow": [{"domain": "myapp", "name": "*"}], "deny": []},
      {"allow": [{"rid": meta:rid, "name": "*"}], "deny": []}
    ) setting(channel)
  fired {
    ent:app_eci := channel{"id"}
  }
}
```

Or raise `wrangler:new_channel_request` with `tags`, `eventPolicy`, and `queryPolicy`. When the channel exists, Wrangler raises `wrangler:channel_created` with the request's attributes plus `channel`, the new channel. Add an attribute of your own to recognize your channel when the event arrives:

```krl
rule ask_for_channel {
  select when myapp channel_needed
  always {
    raise wrangler event "new_channel_request" attributes {
      "tags": ["myapp", "app"],
      "eventPolicy": {"allow": [{"domain": "myapp", "name": "*"}], "deny": []},
      "queryPolicy": {"allow": [{"rid": meta:rid, "name": "*"}], "deny": []},
      "for_rid": meta:rid
    }
  }
}

rule remember_channel {
  select when wrangler channel_created where event:attr("for_rid") == meta:rid
  always {
    ent:app_eci := event:attr("channel"){"id"}
  }
}
```

### Finding channels

`channels()` returns all of this pico's channels. `channels(tags)` returns the channels whose tags are exactly those, in any order and case. The tags can be an array or a comma-separated string. This finds the family channel by which the pico's parent knows it:

```krl
my_child_eci = wrangler:channels("system,child").head(){"id"}
```

`discoveryChannel()` returns the pico's `discovery` channel, which every pico has, for finding out what a pico can do.

### Updating a channel

`updateChannel(eci, tags, eventPolicy, queryPolicy)` replaces a channel's tags and policies and keeps its ECI, so anything that already uses the channel keeps working. Pass the whole policy, not just the change. Or raise `wrangler:channel_update_request` with the same four attributes, and Wrangler raises `wrangler:channel_updated` with the updated `channel`.

### Deleting a channel

`deleteChannel(eci)` deletes a channel. Or raise `wrangler:channel_deletion_request` with the `eci`, and Wrangler raises `wrangler:channel_deleted` with the request's attributes.

### Rotating a channel

If a channel's ECI is being misused, replace it: make a channel with the same tags and policies, give the new ECI to the parties who should have it, and delete the old one. The old ECI then stops working.

```krl
rule rotate_channel {
  select when myapp rotation_needed
  pre {
    old = wrangler:channels(["myapp", "app"]).head()
  }
  if old then every {
    wrangler:createChannel(old{"tags"}, old{"eventPolicy"}, old{"queryPolicy"}) setting(channel)
    wrangler:deleteChannel(old{"id"})
    send_directive("rotated", {"eci": channel{"id"}})
  }
}
```

To change what a channel allows without changing its ECI, update it instead. Pico views have a helper for rotating an app channel, `ui:rotate_app_channel(tags)`; see [Pico views](/pico-views).

## Rulesets

A pico's behavior and state come from its rulesets. A ruleset is KRL source at a URL: `https://`, `file://` on the engine's machine, or the engine's own `/krl/` and `/krl/demos/` paths.

### Installing a ruleset

Raise `wrangler:install_ruleset_request` in one of two forms:

- With `url`: install the KRL at that URL.
- With `absoluteURL` and `rid`: install `<rid>.krl` from the same folder as `absoluteURL`. Pass `meta:rulesetURI` to install a ruleset that sits next to the one asking. An app of several rulesets can be installed this way by a single bootstrap ruleset; see the [Bootstrap and channels](/cookbook/bootstrap/) demo.

Either form takes an optional `config` map, which the installed ruleset reads as `meta:rulesetConfig`, and others can read with `wrangler:rulesetConfig(rid)`.

The engine fetches and compiles the source before installing it. If it doesn't compile, Wrangler raises `wrangler:ruleset_install_failed` with the `url`, `rid`, and the compiler's `errors` and `warnings`. If it installs, and the ruleset wasn't already on this pico, Wrangler raises `wrangler:ruleset_installed` with `rids`, an array holding the installed rid. Installing a ruleset that is already installed updates it to the latest source without raising `ruleset_installed`.

`ruleset_installed` is the first event a newly installed ruleset sees, so it's the place to set up state. Every ruleset on the pico sees the event when any ruleset is installed, so select only your own:

```krl
rule initialize_state {
  select when wrangler ruleset_installed where event:attr("rids") >< meta:rid
  always {
    ent:items := {}
  }
}
```

### Information about installed rulesets

| Function | Returns |
|----------|---------|
| `installedRIDs()` | The rids of the rulesets on this pico |
| `rulesetMeta(rid)` | The ruleset's `meta` block: name, description, author, what it shares, and so on |
| `rulesetConfig(rid)` | The configuration it was installed with |
| `rulesetSchema(rid)` | Its schema: the events its documented rules select and the functions it documents and shares |
| `picoSchema()` | The schemas of all the pico's rulesets, merged |
| `channelSchema(eci)` | What a channel's policy allows, from the pico's schema |
| `rulesetWarnings(rid)` | The compiler's warnings for it |

When the set of rulesets on a pico changes, Wrangler raises `wrangler:schema_updated`.

### Flushing

When a ruleset's source changes, it has to be flushed: fetched and compiled again. Flush one on the **Rulesets** tab of the developer UI. From KRL, raise `wrangler:rulesets_need_flushing` to flush every ruleset on this pico. Wrangler raises `wrangler:rulesets_flushed` when it's done.

The engine compiles each URL once, so a flush affects every pico that installed a ruleset from that URL. Flushing doesn't raise `ruleset_installed` again, so rules that run on install don't run.

### Uninstalling

Raise `wrangler:uninstall_ruleset_request` with a `rid`. Wrangler raises `wrangler:ruleset_uninstalled` with the same attributes. A ruleset that another installed ruleset uses as a module can't be uninstalled.

## Querying other picos

`picoQuery(eci, rid, name, args)` calls a function another pico shares and returns its value:

```krl
rule ask {
  select when myapp question_asked
  pre {
    answer = wrangler:picoQuery(other_eci, "my.ruleset.id", "myFunction", {"arg1": "a"})
  }
  if answer{"error"}.isnull() then noop()
  fired {
    ent:answer := answer
  }
}
```

The target can be an ECI or a DID: a pico's `did:webvh`, or the `did:peer` of an established relationship. On the same engine, `picoQuery` calls the other pico directly. Otherwise it goes over HTTP, or over DIDComm for a DID.

On failure it returns a map with `error`, and for HTTP, `httpStatus` and the other pico's error as `picoQueryError`, `picoQueryErrorMsg`, and `picoQueryReturnValue`.

Optional parameters, for a pico on another engine:

| Parameter | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|
| `_host` | The other engine, with protocol and port, such as `https://picos.example.com`. Defaults to this engine (`meta:host`), and then the query doesn't use HTTP |
| `_path` | The path before the ECI. Default `/sky/cloud/` |
| `_root_url` | The whole URL before the ECI, instead of `_host` and `_path` |

A pico can't query itself: `picoQuery` returns an error ("Pico should not query itself"). A query waits for its answer, so avoid two picos that query each other at the same time. See [Querying another pico](/developing/querying-another-pico).

`skyQuery`, the older version, is still there for old rulesets. It always uses HTTP, which can't use family channels. It takes the same parameters in the same order, so switching to `picoQuery` is a rename.


---

# Wrangler: managing channels

# Managing channels

## What are pico channels?

A pico receives events and answers queries on its channels. A channel is one stream of communication with a pico, and a pico can have any number of them. Each channel has a policy that says which events and queries it accepts.

A channel is identified by its ECI (event channel identifier), a unique string such as `ckiz680qq000a7u2r8myeezof`. To use a channel you need only the ECI and the address of the pico's engine. Then you send events and queries to it [over HTTP](/exp/), or from KRL with `event:send` and `wrangler:picoQuery`. [Relationships](/wrangler/relationships) between picos are built on channels too.

## Why channels

Imagine a pico for a lamp. It lets some parties check whether the lamp is on, and others turn it on and off.

For each party that may control the lamp, the lamp pico makes a channel that accepts `lamp:on` and `lamp:off` events, and gives that party the ECI. For parties that may only check, it makes channels that allow only an `isLampOn` query.

Because each party has its own channel, the lamp pico can restrict or delete one party's channel, say one that flashes the light too fast, without affecting anyone else.

## Kinds of channels

Every channel has an ECI, one or more tags, and a policy. Tags are how you find a channel without knowing its ECI. The policy says what the channel may be used for. A pico's **Channels** tab in the developer UI lists them all.

### Family channels

Family channels have the tag `system`. They can only be used inside the engine, by the right pico, and they allow any event or query from it:

- **Self** (`system, self`): every pico has one, and its ECI is the pico's id. It identifies the pico.
- **Child** (`system, child`): every pico except the root has one. Its parent uses it to send this pico events and queries.
- **Parent** (`system, parent`): a pico has one for each child. The child uses it to reach its parent.

### Other channels Wrangler makes

Every pico also has these:

- **Developer UI** (`engine, ui`): what the developer UI uses for this pico. It allows the UI's own events and queries.
- **Discovery** (`discovery`): lets anyone ask what the pico can do.
- **DIDComm ingress** (`didcomm, ingress`): where DID-based relationship traffic from other engines arrives.
- **Well-known** (`wellknown_rx, tx_rx`): accepts requests for classic (ECI-based) relationships.
- **PDS** (`pds`): `pds` events and `io.picolabs.pds` queries; see [Pico data store](/wrangler/pds).

### External channels

Every other channel can be used by other picos on the same engine, picos on other engines, or any system on the internet. Each external channel defines an API for the pico: the rulesets installed decide what the pico can do, and the channel's policy decides how much of that this channel can reach.

## Creating a channel

### In the developer UI

The **Channels** tab has a form for a new channel: tags, an event policy, and a query policy. The engine assigns the ECI. Check the box beside a channel to see its policies.

For the lamp, one channel might allow `lamp:*` events, for trusted parties. Another might allow only the `isLampOn` query and could be shared more widely. If a party misbehaves, delete its channel and make a new one; give the new ECI only to the parties who should still have it.

### From KRL, synchronously

`wrangler:createChannel(tags, eventPolicy, queryPolicy)` creates a channel and returns it. The ruleset needs `use module io.picolabs.wrangler alias wrangler`.

```krl
rule create_limited_use_channel {
  select when lamp read_only_channel_needed
  pre {
    tags = ["lamp", "read-only"]
    eventPolicy = {"allow": [], "deny": [{"domain": "*", "name": "*"}]}
    queryPolicy = {"allow": [{"rid": meta:rid, "name": "isLampOn"}], "deny": []}
  }
  every {
    wrangler:createChannel(tags, eventPolicy, queryPolicy) setting(channel)
    send_directive("new channel", {"eci": channel{"id"}})
  }
}
```

The directive gives the new ECI to whoever sent the event: a trusted page, say, that builds a link for checking the lamp.

A ruleset often creates its channel when it's installed, from a rule that selects its own `wrangler:ruleset_installed`. See the [Bootstrap and channels](/cookbook/bootstrap/) demo, which also updates the channel instead of making a duplicate when the rule runs again.

### From KRL, asynchronously

Raise `wrangler:new_channel_request`. Any attributes you add are passed through to `wrangler:channel_created`, which carries the new `channel`:

```krl
raise wrangler event "new_channel_request" attributes {
  "tags": ["lamp", "read-only"],
  "eventPolicy": {"allow": [], "deny": [{"domain": "*", "name": "*"}]},
  "queryPolicy": {"allow": [{"rid": meta:rid, "name": "isLampOn"}], "deny": []},
  "co_id": meta:rid
}
```

```krl
rule on_new_channel {
  select when wrangler channel_created where event:attr("co_id") == meta:rid
  pre {
    channel = event:attr("channel").klog("New channel")
  }
  always {
    ent:read_only_eci := channel{"id"}
  }
}
```

The channel looks like this:

```json
{
  "id": "ckj081v5a0093fi2r9es49i77",
  "tags": ["lamp", "read-only"],
  "eventPolicy": {"allow": [], "deny": [{"domain": "*", "name": "*"}]},
  "queryPolicy": {"allow": [{"rid": "lamp_ruleset", "name": "isLampOn"}], "deny": []},
  "familyChannelPicoID": null
}
```

## Updating a channel

Sometimes a channel should change rather than be replaced: tighter or looser policies as trust changes, different tags, or the `oauth-webhook` tag for OAuth client credentials. Updating keeps the ECI, so anything that already uses the channel (links, relationships, stored credentials) keeps working.

Family channels (tagged `system`) can't be updated; the engine manages them. Channels you created can.

### In the developer UI

On the **Channels** tab, check the box beside a channel. Editable channels have an **Edit channel** form: tags (comma-separated, with a shortcut for `oauth-webhook`), and the event and query policies. With the `oauth-webhook` tag, a **Webhook OAuth** panel appears below the form, for creating credentials and minting tokens.

### From KRL, synchronously

`wrangler:updateChannel(eci, tags, eventPolicy, queryPolicy)` replaces the channel's tags and policies and returns the updated channel. All four arguments are required: it replaces, it doesn't merge, so pass the whole policies even to change one thing. This adds the `oauth-webhook` tag and keeps the rest:

```krl
rule protect_webhook_channel {
  select when myapp webhook_protection_needed
  pre {
    eci = event:attr("eci")
    chann = wrangler:channels().filter(function(c) { c{"id"} == eci }).head()
  }
  if chann then every {
    wrangler:updateChannel(eci, chann{"tags"}.append("oauth-webhook"), chann{"eventPolicy"}, chann{"queryPolicy"}) setting(updated)
    send_directive("channel updated", {"eci": updated{"id"}, "tags": updated{"tags"}})
  }
}
```

Adding `oauth-webhook` makes the channel require an access token. Until you create credentials for it, in the developer UI or with [`io.picolabs.oauth`](/wrangler/oauth), outside requests on it are refused.

### From KRL, asynchronously

Raise `wrangler:channel_update_request` with `eci`, `tags`, `eventPolicy`, and `queryPolicy`. Wrangler raises `wrangler:channel_updated`, with your attributes passed through and the updated `channel`.

### Update, or delete and recreate?

To revoke a party's access, deleting the channel and making a new one is simplest. To change what a channel allows, while the people using it keep using it, update it.

## Deleting a channel

`wrangler:deleteChannel(eci)` deletes a channel. Or raise `wrangler:channel_deletion_request` with its `eci`:

```krl
raise wrangler event "channel_deletion_request" attributes {"eci": old_eci, "co_id": meta:rid}
```

Wrangler raises `wrangler:channel_deleted` with the same attributes. To delete channels by their tags, find them first with `wrangler:channels(tags)`.

## Channel attributes

| Attribute | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|
| `id` | The ECI: a globally unique identifier. Anyone who knows it and can reach the engine can send the channel events and queries, so treat it as a capability |
| `tags` | One or more tags, for finding the channel. `wrangler:channels(tags)` finds the channels with exactly those tags |
| `eventPolicy` | Which events the channel accepts |
| `queryPolicy` | Which queries the channel accepts |

## Policies

A policy has an `allow` list and a `deny` list. An event policy's rules name a `domain` and a `name`; a query policy's rules name a `rid` and a `name`. Every rule needs both fields, and `"*"` matches anything. An event or query is accepted if it matches a rule in `allow` and none in `deny`. `deny` wins.

Allow only `foo:bar`:

```json
"eventPolicy": {
  "allow": [{"domain": "foo", "name": "bar"}],
  "deny": []
}
```

Allow every `foo` event except `foo:bar`, and also `aaa:bbb`:

```json
"eventPolicy": {
  "allow": [
    {"domain": "foo", "name": "*"},
    {"domain": "aaa", "name": "bbb"}
  ],
  "deny": [
    {"domain": "foo", "name": "bar"}
  ]
}
```

| Event | Result |
|-------|--------|
| `foo:foo`, `foo:wat` | Allowed |
| `foo:bar` | Denied: it matches `deny` |
| `aaa:bbb` | Allowed |
| `aaa:ccc`, `zzz:wat` | Denied: nothing in `allow` matches |

Allow everything except `system` events and `danger:nuke`:

```json
"eventPolicy": {
  "allow": [{"domain": "*", "name": "*"}],
  "deny": [
    {"domain": "system", "name": "*"},
    {"domain": "danger", "name": "nuke"}
  ]
}
```

Query policies work the same way, with `rid` instead of `domain`. A channel that allows everything:

```json
{
  "eventPolicy": {"allow": [{"domain": "*", "name": "*"}], "deny": []},
  "queryPolicy": {"allow": [{"rid": "*", "name": "*"}], "deny": []}
}
```

Give each channel the least it needs. A pico's schema can build a policy that allows exactly its documented API; see the [Bootstrap and channels](/cookbook/bootstrap/) demo and `wrangler:channelSchema(eci)`.

## Using channels

- **Over HTTP**: events at `/sky/event/<eci>/...` and queries at `/sky/query/<eci>/...`. See the [Event Exchange Protocol](/exp/).
- **`event:send`**, from KRL, to a channel on this engine or another.
- **`wrangler:picoQuery`**, from KRL, to call a function on another pico. See [The wrangler ruleset](/wrangler/wrangler).
- **The developer UI's Testing tab**, which sends events and queries on a channel you pick.
- **`raise`** in a postlude, which is handled on the same pico, as if it came in on the channel of the event being handled (`meta:eci`).

For every channel event and function, see the [wrangler API reference](/rulesets/io.picolabs.wrangler).


---

# Wrangler: relationships

# Relationships

*For KRL developers and engine operators. Engine 1.6 and later (DID-based relationships); the classic ECI path is still supported. Ruleset: `io.picolabs.subscription`, installed on every pico.*

A relationship is a pairwise connection between two picos. Before engine 1.6.2, relationships were called subscriptions. Relationships are formed with `wrangler:relationship` (or the older `wrangler:subscription`). Their state lives in `io.picolabs.subscription`, which keeps that name for compatibility.

New rulesets can load it under the new name:

```krl
use module io.picolabs.subscription alias relationship
```

| Prefer (1.6.2 and later) | Still works |
|--------------------------|-------------|
| `wrangler:relationship` | `wrangler:subscription` |
| `relationship:established()` (module alias) | `subscription:established()` |
| The **Relationships** tab | The `/subscriptions` URL |

## What is a relationship?

The two picos in a relationship may be in the same mesh, in different meshes, or on different engines. A parent and its children talk through family channels and don't need one. Relationships are for picos that aren't related that way, such as your pico and a community pico, two peer meshes, or a service and its clients, so they can exchange events and queries under explicit channel policy.

Each side keeps a relationship record: who the other party is, how to reach it, and which local channel (`Rx`) enforces what the other party may do. A relationship goes from outbound pending (on the side that asked) and inbound pending (on the side asked) to established, when both sides agree.

## Identity: three identifiers

Since engine 1.6, relationships use two kinds of DID as well as ECIs:

| Identifier | Role | When you use it |
|------------|------|-----------------|
| `did:webvh` | The pico's portable identity: who the actor is | To start a DID-based relationship (`target_did`); public intro |
| `did:peer` | The relationship's private identity, for this pair | After the introduction is approved, for ongoing encrypted traffic |
| ECI (channel id) | The local policy gate on this engine | The `Rx` channel on each pico; the other side's `Tx` ECI in classic relationships |

New relationships use DIDs; ECIs are for existing applications. Use the `did:webvh` for introductions and `did:peer` for everything after. Don't start a new relationship with a peer DID or a well-known ECI.

Every pico publishes its `did:webvh` at `GET /picos/{picoId}/did.jsonl`. In KRL it's `wrangler:myDid()`; in the developer UI, it's in the **Relationships** tab's **Identity** panel. To be reached across meshes or engines by its DID, a pico needs **public intro** turned on.

## The lifecycle

| State | The side that asked | The side asked |
|-------|---------------------|----------------|
| Outbound pending | Waiting for the other side | — |
| Inbound pending | — | Approve or ignore |
| Established | Connected | Connected |

## DID-based relationships (recommended)

DID-based relationships are the default for new work. They form with an introduction handshake, and the established relationship stores `Tx_did` and `Rx_did` instead of the other side's ECI.

### Forming one

The side that asks raises `wrangler:relationship`:

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| `layer2` | `true` |
| `target_did` | The other pico's `did:webvh` (`wrangler:myDid()` there, or from its UI) |
| `name` | Optional label, shown in the established list |
| `Tx_role`, `Rx_role` | Optional roles: the other side's and this side's |
| `channel_type` | Usually `Tx_Rx` |

The side asked approves with `wrangler:pending_relationship_approval`, or by an auto-accept rule (see [Accepting relationship requests](/developing/accepting-relationship-requests)).

Don't pass `wellKnown_Tx` on a DID-based request, or a `did:peer`: the engine makes the pairwise DIDs during the introduction.

| You have the other pico's… | DID-based request | Classic request |
|-----------------------------|-------------------|-----------------|
| `did:webvh` | ✅ `target_did` | ❌ |
| `wellKnown_Rx` ECI | ❌ | ✅ `wellKnown_Tx` |
| `did:peer` | ❌ | ❌ |

On the same engine, the engine resolves the `did:webvh` locally and runs the introduction without HTTP.

### The established relationship

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `Id` | The relationship's id, the same on both sides |
| `name` | Its label |
| `layer2` | `true` |
| `Tx_did` | The other side's `did:peer` |
| `Rx_did` | This side's `did:peer` for this relationship |
| `Rx` | This side's ECI: where policy is enforced |
| `Tx_host` | Set when the other pico is on another engine |

### Sending queries and events

Query the other pico by DID, or through the relationship:

```krl
// By DID: wrangler finds the established relationship
wrangler:picoQuery(other_did, "io.picolabs.wrangler", "id", {})

// By relationship Id
relationship:queryOnSub(sub_id, "io.picolabs.wrangler", "id", {})
```

Send an event by DID, or with the relationship record:

```krl
event:send({"did": other_did, "domain": "myapp", "type": "ping", "attrs": {}})
event:send({"sub": bus, "domain": "myapp", "type": "ping", "attrs": {}})
```

For a DID-based relationship, the engine delivers locally when both picos are in the same mesh on this engine, and otherwise over DIDComm to the other pico's ingress.

## How traffic is routed

How a query or event reaches the other pico depends on three things: whether the relationship is DID-based or classic, whether the two picos are in the same mesh (the same passkey root on one engine), and whether the other pico is on this engine. Wherever it comes from, the other side's access is checked on this side's `Rx` channel.

| Relationship | Kind | Transport | Policy |
|--------------|------|-----------|--------|
| Parent and child | None (family) | Local | Family channel |
| Same mesh, same engine | DID-based or classic | Local | The relationship's `Rx` channel |
| Different meshes, same engine | DID-based | DIDComm to the ingress | The relationship's `Rx` channel |
| Different engines | DID-based | DIDComm to the other engine | The relationship's `Rx` channel |
| Classic | Classic | HTTP or `event:send` to `Tx` | `Tx` and `Rx` policies |

OAuth integrators are a separate path: HTTP to `/sky/*` with a bearer token, not a relationship.

To change what the other side may do, edit the `Rx` channel's policy on the **Channels** tab, or expand the relationship on the **Relationships** tab and follow its link to the channel.

## Across engines

- Each engine needs a stable address that the other can reach, `PICO_ENGINE_BASE_URL`. It is built into each pico's `did:webvh` when the pico is created.
- The side asked (often a root pico) has public intro on. Root picos default to on; child picos to off.
- The side that asks uses the other's `did:webvh` as `target_did`.

The handshake is the same as on one engine, but the introduction, its response, and the traffic after use encrypted DIDComm to `POST {peerBase}/sky/event/{ingressEci}/none/dido/didcomm_message`.

### Two engines on one machine

```sh
# Terminal 1
PICO_ENGINE_HOME=/tmp/pico-engine-a PORT=3001 npm start
# Terminal 2
PICO_ENGINE_HOME=/tmp/pico-engine-b PORT=3002 npm start
```

1. Register a passkey on both developer UIs.
2. On engine B, **Relationships** → **Identity**: copy the `did:webvh`.
3. On engine A, **Relationships** → **New relationship** (DID-based): paste B's DID and submit.
4. On B, under **Inbound pending**, approve it.
5. On A, the established relationship shows `Tx_did`, `Rx_did`, and `Tx_host`.

### Debugging

| Symptom | Check |
|---------|-------|
| The introduction never arrives | Public intro on the side asked; ports and firewalls |
| DID resolution failed | Fetch `{base}/picos/{id}/did.jsonl` |
| 401 on DIDComm | Approve the relationship again; check that the ingress channel exists |

## Classic (ECI-based) relationships

The original relationship model is still fully supported for existing rulesets and tutorials:

- The side asked has a well-known channel, `wellKnown_Rx` (shown in the **Identity** panel).
- The side that asks raises `wrangler:relationship` with `wellKnown_Tx` set to that ECI, and no `layer2`.
- The established relationship has `Tx` and `Rx` ECIs, and `layer2` is false.

The [Two picos talking](/cookbook/two_picos/) and [Collection](/cookbook/collection/) demos use classic relationships.

## The Relationships tab

The developer UI's **Relationships** tab manages a pico's relationships:

- **Identity**: the pico's `did:webvh`, with a copy button; the classic `wellKnown_Rx` ECI; and the **Public intro** checkbox.
- **Established**, **Inbound pending**, and **Outbound pending** lists. Expand a row to see its DIDs and `Rx` policy, send a test event, approve, cancel, or delete it.
- **New relationship**: DID-based or classic, with `target_did` or `wellKnown_Tx`, `name`, `Rx_role`, `Tx_role`, `channel_type`, and an optional password.

Give relationships names, so the lists stay readable. The `Id` is still shown, for debugging.

## The KRL API

Relationships live in two rulesets on every pico. `io.picolabs.subscription` keeps the relationship records and runs most of the lifecycle. `io.picolabs.wrangler` has the identity functions and `picoQuery`. You raise `wrangler` events to create, approve, and cancel relationships, and query `io.picolabs.subscription` for their state.

### Identity

| Function or event | Purpose |
|-------------------|---------|
| `wrangler:myDid()` | This pico's `did:webvh`: give it to the other side as its `target_did` |
| `wrangler:publicIntro()` | Whether this pico accepts introductions on its DID |
| `wrangler:set_public_intro` event, with `enabled` | Turn public intro on or off |
| `wrangler:callerDid()` | On an incoming cross-pico event, the sender's `did:webvh`, when the engine has it |

### Reading relationships

| Function | Returns |
|----------|---------|
| `relationship:established()` | The established relationships |
| `relationship:established("Tx_role", "owner")` | Only those whose field matches (any field works) |
| `relationship:inbound()` | Requests waiting for this pico's approval |
| `relationship:outbound()` | Requests waiting for the other side |
| `relationship:wellKnown_Rx()` | The well-known channel, for classic relationships |
| `relationship:autoAcceptConfig()` | The auto-accept rules |

Each relationship is a map with `Id`, `name`, `Tx_role`, `Rx_role`, the local `Rx`, and either `Tx_did` and `Rx_did` (DID-based) or `Tx` and `Tx_host` (classic).

### Creating a relationship

DID-based:

```krl
raise wrangler event "relationship" attributes {
  "layer2": true,
  "target_did": other_did,
  "name": "battery-monitor",
  "Rx_role": "sensor",
  "Tx_role": "controller",
  "channel_type": "Tx_Rx"
}
```

Classic:

```krl
raise wrangler event "relationship" attributes {
  "wellKnown_Tx": other_well_known_eci,
  "name": "legacy-link",
  "Rx_role": "client",
  "Tx_role": "server"
}
```

Either takes an optional `password`, if the other side's auto-accept configuration uses one. The relationship ruleset creates the local `Rx` channel, records the outbound request, and runs the handshake.

### Approving, rejecting, and canceling

| Event | When | Key attributes |
|-------|------|----------------|
| `wrangler:pending_relationship_approval` | Accept an inbound request | `Id` (or `Rx` or `Tx`) |
| `wrangler:inbound_rejection` | Decline an inbound request | `Id` |
| `wrangler:outbound_cancellation` | Withdraw an outbound request | `Id` |
| `wrangler:relationship_cancellation` | End an established relationship | `Id` |

Each raises companion events that other rulesets can select, such as `wrangler:relationship_added` and `wrangler:relationship_removed` (and their older names, `subscription_added` and `subscription_removed`).

### Talking to the other pico

1. `wrangler:picoQuery(target, rid, name, args)`, where the target is a `did:webvh`, a `did:peer`, or a classic `Tx` ECI. The engine finds the established relationship and routes the query.
2. `relationship:queryOnSub(Id, rid, name, args)`, by relationship `Id`.
3. `event:send({"did": ..., ...})` or `event:send({"sub": relationship, ...})`.
4. To several relationships at once, raise `wrangler:send_event_on_subs` with a `subID`, or a `Tx_role` or `Rx_role`, and the `domain`, `type`, and `attrs` to send.

### Quick reference

| Goal | API |
|------|-----|
| This pico's portable DID | `wrangler:myDid()` |
| List established relationships | `relationship:established()` |
| Start a DID-based relationship | `wrangler:relationship` with `layer2` and `target_did` |
| Start a classic relationship | `wrangler:relationship` with `wellKnown_Tx` |
| Approve a request | `wrangler:pending_relationship_approval` with `Id` |
| End a relationship | `wrangler:relationship_cancellation` with `Id` |
| Query the other pico | `wrangler:picoQuery(did, rid, name, args)` or `relationship:queryOnSub(...)` |
| Send it an event | `event:send({"did": ...})` or `event:send({"sub": relationship, ...})` |

Authorization is the same for both kinds: the other side's access is enforced on your `Rx` channel's event and query policy. DID-based relationships change how messages are addressed, not who is allowed.

## Public intro

Public intro decides whether a pico accepts an unsolicited introduction: someone starting a DID-based relationship by sending an introduction to its `did:webvh`, without a well-known channel. That matters across engines and meshes, where the asking side may know only the DID. With public intro off, the engine drops the introduction, and it never reaches the inbound pending list.

It answers "may strangers introduce themselves by DID?" It doesn't replace approval: after an introduction arrives, you still approve it (unless auto-accept matches), and the `Rx` policy still governs what the other pico may do.

Root picos default to on, so other engines can reach your mesh's root by DID. Child picos default to off.

| How | What to do |
|-----|------------|
| Developer UI | **Relationships** → **Identity** → **Public intro** |
| Query | `wrangler:publicIntro()` |
| Event | `raise wrangler event "set_public_intro" attributes {"enabled": true}` |

Leave it on for root picos that should receive requests from other engines, and for picos that partners will reach by DID. Turn it off for picos that should be reached only through their parent or a classic well-known channel, or that you don't want to be discoverable by DID.

Once a DID-based relationship is established, public intro can be turned off: the relationship uses its `did:peer` from then on.

## Roles and policy

`Tx_role` and `Rx_role` describe each side's part, such as `controller` or `member`. They label relationships; they don't prove anything. Authorization is the local `Rx` channel's policy, as it always was. Frameworks such as Manifold confer rights through relationships plus channel policy; DID-based relationships change how you address the other pico, not how policy works.

## Not yet implemented

- Migrating classic relationships to DID-based ones automatically (create new relationships instead)
- Authorization based on verifiable credentials over relationships
- `did:peer:4` (engine 1.6 uses `num_algo` 2)

Moving a pico to another engine is implemented: its `did:webvh` and its DID-based relationships move with it. See [Portable subtrees](/wrangler/portable-subtree).

## Related pages

- [Engine 1.6 release notes](/release/1.6)
- [Managing channels](/wrangler/channels): `Rx` policy
- [Identity libraries](/design/pico-identity-libraries) and [relationships design](/design/pico-relationships)
- [SKY over DIDComm](/design/sky-didcomm-protocol)
